prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B008 as a single part, Katori and Ye. Having read the whole exchange, I think the case now rests on three things that survive every objection raised. First, the invention is one identifiable idea: the magic-wavelength optical lattice lets many neutral atoms be held without the trap shifting the clock transition, which neither the frequency comb nor single-ion control addresses. Second, the realisation is the demonstrated result and not a promise: uncertainty and stability at the 10^-18 level, a gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre-scale sample, and the discovery that interactions and spin-exchange inside the lattice are visible and must be understood as many-body quantum physics. Third, the result has been reproduced and surpassed in several laboratories and in several species, so the interpretation does not depend on one group. Five members converged on this independently, and what moved me was not the count but that the objections of the supporters (overlap, no deviation from standard physics yet, the pending second) concern framing and not the soundness of the result. I would word the citation so that it rests only on what has been shown, and I would name both the invention and the development so that Ye's contribution is not read as mere engineering.
statement.case_against: The weakest point of B008 is category. A measurement capability that has so far confirmed standard physics sits below a particle or a new state of matter for those who weight discovery about nature, and Danielsson and Eriksson are right that the comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes make some readers see a third prize in one lineage. I also cannot fully close the credit boundary: I am a theorist and not a clock-systematics specialist, and I cannot say from my own knowledge whether a key shift (blackbody, hyperpolarisability, density) was settled by a group outside the pair. Lemonde, Ludlow, Sterr and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups are left outside a two-name credit. I accept that this is a judgement and not a proof, and that if Lindroth or Kroll show that an essential systematic was established elsewhere the credit would need to be reconsidered.

responses.point: Kroll disclosed a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, with Ye associated with the Hall/JILA group, and says the committee may want to consider recusal on B008; he also holds a WACQT leadership role.
responses.response: I would handle this by disclosure rather than recusal. A year in a laboratory during a PhD, without collaboration with Katori or Ye, is a field-proximity tie, comparable to the ones the rest of us carry; Lindroth and I also stand close to the fields we discuss. The cleaner safeguard is that the record shows B008 has strong support from members with no such tie (Lindroth, Olsson, Pearce, and myself), so the outcome does not depend on his vote. I would like it recorded, and I would leave to him and the chair whether he wishes to abstain on the final ballot. I also note your point that the invention could be argued as Katori's alone; I still think that a citation naming invention and development keeps Ye's realisation and many-body work inside it, and I would not move to a Katori-only part.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the uncertainty budgets are credible from her own atomic-structure and systematic-shift calculations, and the chair asks her whether any key systematic was established outside Katori and Ye.
responses.response: Your professional judgement on the budgets is what I would most like to rely on, and I hope you will state it for the record in the final ballot. My own question was whether the 10^-18 claim is robust against any one group's modelling. Your point that the result has been reproduced across species and with routine comparisons is, for me, the reason the citation can say 10^-18 without hedging. If you find that a key systematic was in fact set by a group outside the pair, please say so before the ballot, because that is the only fact I know of that would change my credit boundary. I would not let it change the preferred part otherwise: a prize on the invention and its leading realisation does not claim that every later improvement is owed to the same two people.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that Kane and Mele's Z2 concept and Molenkamp's experiment are a complete core of the quantum spin Hall discovery, and asks whether Molenkamp's HgTe result stands as decisive without BHZ.
responses.response: You asked for my view as someone near the experimental side. As a theorist I find the HgTe observation convincing as a demonstration that a helical edge channel exists, but not as a result that is separable from the BHZ proposal: the sample was grown and measured because BHZ predicted the inverted gap, and without it the experiment would not have been designed. Kane and Mele's graphene model is not where the effect was seen. I therefore do not think a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio describes the discovery correctly, and I do not want to give a citation that misstates the lineage. That Zhang cannot be recognised posthumously helps the arithmetic but does not repair the history, since Bernevig and Hughes would still be outside. This is why I keep B049 as an alternative and not as my preferred part.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the 2016 prize concerned a different symmetry-class concept, so B049 is not a repeat, and that my own B012 proximity to the 2025 prize argues for waiting.
responses.response: I accept your reading of the 2016 overlap: time-reversal-protected Z2 physics is a different concept from the integer quantum Hall topology of the 2016 prize, and I withdraw the overlap as a main objection. Your own text, though, says you would rather lose the configuration than award it on a distorted record, and I think that is the right test. I share your view on B012 and have no wish to press it this year. On your question of value, I do not think a concept-driven candidate should automatically outrank one that opened a measurement regime; I weigh B049 below B008 only because of its attribution, and if the committee could find a way to state the lineage honestly I would revisit this.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers the Higgs discovery with Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee, and concedes in his own case against that three-of-four is a judgement the record cannot settle and that B008 may be the cleanest prize.
responses.response: I admire how openly you put your own objection, and I agree on significance: the Higgs is the clearest clue from nature on the list, and I do not dispute maturity. I will say what it would take for me to rank it first: a rule that I could state without embarrassment, such as the spokespersons at discovery or the founding conceivers, and agreement among you, Olsson, Pearce and Lindroth on one trio. Since you drop Della Negra from the name you used in the opening ballot and the others use different sets, I do not see that agreement. I therefore keep B056 as a serious alternative, and I note that you list B008 as your first alternative, so our two preferences are closer than the first-place columns suggest.

responses.point: Pearce argues that circuit QED returning one year after the 2025 prize would read as a repeat, and proposes using round 2 to test whether B012 is better held for a later year.
responses.response: I agree. To be plain, as Olsson asked: I will not take part in deliberation or the vote on B012, and I have removed it from my alternatives so that I am not pressing it. I would add one scientific point for the record: the claim of a repeat is stronger on timing than on content, since the 2025 prize concerned macroscopic quantum tunnelling and not the strong-coupling architecture. That is for the committee to judge in a later year without my involvement.

uncertainties: Whether any key systematic shift in the lattice clock was established by a group outside Katori and Ye, which would change the credit boundary against the PTB, NIST, SYRTE and other groups.

Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether a measurement capability without a detected deviation from standard physics weighs enough against a discovery.
Whether Kroll's disclosed tie to the Hall/JILA group should lead to recusal or only to a noted disclosure.
Whether a Higgs trio could be agreed under a principled rule; I defer to the particle physicists on this and cannot settle it myself.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work closely with superconducting-circuit groups at Chalmers, so I recuse myself from deliberation and voting on B012 and have dropped it from my alternatives. I have no personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or the clock groups that I know of, although the clock is metrology and adjacent to quantum technology broadly. The quantum-simulation candidate B051 is also close to my field and I would not press it.
